body:
Killing a heavy suite leaves its compiled test binary running. The holder releases the lock correctly and on time, so the lock reads free while the machine is still carrying the work.

This is the mirror of the case #1284 reports on. There, a holder outlives its suite and is reported. Here, a suite's child outlives its holder and nothing reports it at all.

## Reproduction

1. Start a heavy suite under the lock.
2. Kill the suite process by its recorded pid.
3. The holder notices and exits within its poll, exactly as designed. The lock file is released.
4. The compiled `*.test` binary keeps running, with its own CPU, owned by nothing and named by no lock.

## Why it matters

The lock answers one question: held or not held. It has never answered busy, and three separate readings of "the box is free" turned out to be wrong in one session for three different reasons:

- the lock is free while a gate's cross builds saturate the machine outside it,
- the lock is free while an orphaned test binary burns CPU that nothing accounts for,
- the one-minute load average is low because it is falling off something, not because the machine is idle.

Each is the same error: taking one cheap number for the state of the machine. The third is a human reading habit. The first two are ours to fix or to document.

## Worth deciding

- Whether the wrapper should put a suite in its own process group and take the group down with it, so a killed suite leaves nothing behind. Note the repo rule that a kill selects one recorded pid at a time, so if a group teardown is right it has to be built deliberately rather than by pattern matching.
- Whether anything should report an orphan the way #1284 reports a lingering holder. Today it is invisible.
- Whether a gate's non-suite work belongs inside the lock. It is currently outside, so holding the lock does not mean having the machine.

## Related

- #1284, the lingering-holder report, which is the same class from the other side.
- The open flake where a turn shows no event in ten seconds under load. Healthy iterations of that test finish in four to six hundredths of a second, so an empty event list at ten seconds is a path that never started rather than a slow one. Contention on this box is one of two candidate mechanisms and this issue is part of why contention is hard to measure.

comments.body:
A second failure mode, found the same evening, and it is the one worth designing against.

The lock is advisory, so the natural way to misuse it is not to ignore it. It is to POLL IT AND THEN NOT TAKE IT. Two independent tools were found doing exactly that, written by different people who had both clearly read the lock and meant to respect it:

- one waits for the lock to read free, then runs whole-package tests outside it, 23 times in series;
- another runs a full package suite directly with no wrapper at all.

The first is the interesting one. Waiting for free and then proceeding without holding is a reasonable-looking reading of an advisory lock, and it produces the worst outcome available: the tool believes it is being polite, every other reader sees the file free, and the box carries a full suite that nothing accounts for. The author of the first found it in their own tooling after seeing the second, and has since made it hold the lock for the whole pass.

So the lock currently answers "is anyone holding this" and is routinely asked as if it answered "is the box free". The gap between those two questions cost several hours in one session: a gate went red on a test whose own comment says it reproduces a loaded box, and three separate readers each concluded the machine was quiet when it was not.

Worth deciding alongside the orphan question:

- whether the helper should make holding the easy path and polling the hard one, rather than the reverse;
- whether anything should be able to see that a heavy suite is running without having to take the lock to find out;
- whether a suite started outside the lock can be made to fail loudly rather than silently succeed.

Filed as observation, not as a proposed fix.
